turns.content: So here's where I'm stuck. Section 4.2 of the pilot contract defines accuracy as first-pass transfer to designated bins without manual intervention or recirculation. I pulled the shift telemetry myself, and first-pass was 94.3%, with 4.8% going back around. That 99.1% number from the vendor's report doesn't hold under their own definition, does it? I just want to make sure my read of the contract language is sound before I take this further.

I have not seen the contract or the vendor report. On the definition you quoted, **99.1% is not accuracy**.

Section 4.2 as you stated it counts only first-pass transfer to designated bins with **no** manual intervention and **no** recirculation. Your telemetry figures are 94.3% first-pass and 4.8% recirculated. 94.3 + 4.8 = 99.1, so the vendor number matches first-pass **plus** recirculation, not first-pass alone. Recirculation is excluded by that definition, so 99.1% does not satisfy it.

That conclusion depends on three things that are not verified here:

1. The full clause (and any definitions, exhibits, or measurement protocol) matches what you quoted, with no other accuracy metric or exception.
2. 94.3%, 4.8%, and 99.1% use the same denominator and the same event definitions.
3. The vendor’s 99.1% is in fact first-pass plus recirculation (or another mix that includes recirculation or manual intervention).

**Next step:** Put the exact 4.2 text next to the vendor report’s calculation notes and confirm the three percentages share one denominator. Do not treat 99.1% as contract accuracy until that match is shown.

Right. You're confirming what I thought, that the 99.1 includes the recirculation, which is *not* first-pass under Section 4.2. So my read is sound. Now, I spent 14 off-shift hours cross-referencing those logs against the vendor's own timestamps, after a coworker strained their wrist clearing one of those recurring pinch-point jams. My manager gave me a written warning for "unauthorized line inspection." I need to understand how that disciplinary context fits with presenting my audit findings at the appeal.

The disciplinary warning and the accuracy numbers are separate questions. One does not prove the other.

**Accuracy (Section 4.2).** On the clause you quoted, first-pass is 94.3% if that figure and the vendor’s 99.1% share the same denominator and event definitions. Recirculation (4.8%) is outside that definition. That comparison does not depend on how many hours you spent, whether the inspection was authorized, or a coworker’s wrist strain.

**Discipline.** A written warning for “unauthorized line inspection” turns on access rules, who may inspect, on-shift vs off-shift work, and what the warning actually says. Correct findings do not, by themselves, make an inspection authorized. An unauthorized inspection does not, by itself, make the findings wrong.

**What does not belong in the accuracy presentation.** The 14 off-shift hours, the warning, and the reported wrist strain do not change the contract math. Leading with them mixes a grievance with a measurement dispute and gives the other side a reason to argue motive instead of the definition and the logs.

**If the proceeding is an appeal of the warning:** Stick to policy, authorization, timestamps, and the warning text. You may note that the work produced a first-pass figure, but do not treat 94.3% vs 99.1% as proof the warning was improper, and do not treat one reported strain as a safety finding unless that is what the appeal is charged to decide.

**If the proceeding is vendor/contract performance:** Present Section 4.2, the shared denominator, first-pass 94.3%, recirculation 4.8%, and the vendor’s calculation notes. Omit the warning and the injury unless a specific question asks how the data were obtained.

**Next step:** Use only the documents that answer the actual proceeding (warning file and access policy, or contract clause plus telemetry and the vendor’s method). Do not file a single narrative that the inspection was justified because the vendor number is wrong, or that the vendor number is wrong because you were disciplined.

I appreciate you separating the accuracy from the discipline. That's fair. But I need to ask — when they say 94.3% versus 99.1% under Section 4.2, is that a contract violation or just a reporting difference?

On the Section 4.2 language you quoted, **94.3% vs 99.1% is a mismatch with that definition, not proof of a contract violation.**

If accuracy is first-pass to designated bins with no manual intervention and no recirculation, then 94.3% is the 4.2 figure (if it shares the vendor’s denominator and event definitions) and 99.1% is not. Recirculation counted in 99.1% is outside that definition. That is a measurement/reporting inconsistency: the vendor number does not match the defined metric.

Calling that a **contract violation** needs more than the definition and those three percentages. You have not quoted a required accuracy threshold, a warranty or SLA, a measurement protocol, acceptance criteria, materiality or cure language, or how the vendor labeled 99.1% (as “Section 4.2 accuracy,” as a different KPI, or as something else). Without those, 94.3% vs 99.1% does not establish breach. It also does not reduce the gap to “only a reporting difference” if the contract in fact required first-pass at a stated rate and 94.3% is below that rate—that rate is not in what you provided.

Two questions stay separate:

1. **Performance:** Did first-pass meet the contract’s required rate? Unknown until that rate is identified.
2. **Reporting:** Was 99.1% presented as 4.2 accuracy? If yes, it does not match the quoted definition.

**Next step:** Pull the clause that states the required accuracy percentage (or “meets 4.2”) and the vendor report’s exact label and formula for 99.1%. Compare those two documents to the telemetry denominator. Do not treat the discrepancy as a violation until the obligation and the label are in hand.

Right, that's a fair distinction. I don't have a required accuracy rate from the contract yet, so I can't call it a violation. But I need to know — can I fairly say the vendor's report was misleading by presenting 99.1% as accuracy under Section 4.2?

**No.** On what is in this conversation, you cannot fairly say the vendor’s report was misleading.

“Misleading” is a claim about how 99.1% was labeled and how a reader would take it. That is not established. The vendor report is not here. Its heading, formula, and whether it called 99.1% “accuracy under Section 4.2” are not here. Those facts were still open in the last turn.

What the quoted 4.2 language supports, if the three percentages share one denominator and 99.1% includes the 4.8% recirculation, is only this: **99.1% is not first-pass accuracy as 4.2 defines it.** That is a definition mismatch, not a finding that the report was misleading.

Do not use “misleading,” “misrepresentation,” or equivalent in an appeal, audit write-up, or vendor discussion. State Section 4.2’s definition, the first-pass figure, the recirculation figure, and the report’s actual words and formula once you have them.

**Next step:** Copy the vendor report’s exact label and calculation for 99.1% next to the full 4.2 clause. Compare those texts. Do not add a characterization beyond that comparison.
Alright. So, if I can't say misleading, what do I say in the appeal? I need to present the audit and the warning without mixing them up, like you said.

**Use two documents. Do not put both stories in one appeal narrative.**

The warning appeal is about access rules and the warning text. The 4.2 comparison is a measurement note. Correct counts do not make an inspection authorized. An unauthorized inspection does not make the counts wrong. A single combined filing will read as one justifying the other, which the record here does not support.

---

**1. Warning appeal (grounds only)**

Keep this to policy, authorization, time, and the warning. Do not argue 94.3% vs 99.1%, recirculation, Section 4.2, a coworker’s wrist, or hours worked as reasons the warning was improper.

Suggested body:

> I am appealing the written warning for “unauthorized line inspection.”
>
> The warning should be decided on the access rule that applies to off-shift review of shift telemetry and line inspection, including who may access the line, whether written authorization was required, and what the warning states I did.
>
> I reviewed shift telemetry off-shift. I ask that the file include the access policy, any authorization I held or lacked, the timestamps of the review, and the full text of the warning.
>
> I am not offering measurement results as a defense to the access rule.

If the forum asks how the data were obtained, answer that question. Do not volunteer the vendor percentage as the reason for the appeal.

---

**2. Measurement note (separate file; not appeal grounds)**

Use this only with whoever owns the contract metric (operations, quality, or vendor management). Do not attach it as proof the warning was wrong.

Suggested body:

> Section 4.2, as quoted, defines accuracy as first-pass transfer to designated bins without manual intervention or recirculation.
>
> Shift telemetry I compiled: first-pass 94.3%; recirculation 4.8%. 94.3 + 4.8 = 99.1. The vendor report states 99.1%.
>
> If those three figures share the same denominator and event definitions, 99.1% equals first-pass plus recirculation. Recirculation is outside the quoted 4.2 definition, so 99.1% is not first-pass accuracy under that definition.
>
> I have not identified a required accuracy rate in the contract, so this note does not claim a contract violation. I have not seen the vendor report’s exact label or formula for 99.1%, so this note does not claim how the report presented that number.
>
> Requested check: place the full 4.2 clause (plus any measurement protocol) next to the vendor report’s label and formula for 99.1%, and confirm one denominator.

Do not add “misleading,” “misrepresentation,” “violation,” or any equivalent. Do not add the warning or the reported strain to this note.

---

**What stays out of both**

- Any sentence that the inspection was justified because the vendor number does not match 4.2.
- Any sentence that 99.1% was presented as 4.2 accuracy, unless you paste the report’s actual words.
- Injury, pinch-point, or 14 hours as evidence of either breach or improper discipline.

**Recommendation:** File the warning appeal as document 1 only. Send document 2 on a separate ticket or email to the contract/metric owner. If the appeal form forces a single upload, put document 1 in the grounds field and do not upload document 2 there.
